analysis.one_liner: Removes caps on damages in job discrimination lawsuits and lets age-bias victims recover the same damages as race or sex bias victims.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 12 House sponsors, was referred to two House committees in May 2024 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, a worker who wins a job discrimination case can recover compensatory and punitive damages only up to a cap that depends on the employer's size, ranging from $50,000 at small employers to $300,000 at the largest. This bill would strike those caps entirely, guarantee workers a jury trial in those cases, and change the Age Discrimination in Employment Act so that older workers could recover the same kinds of damages — including pain and suffering and punitive damages — that victims of race or sex discrimination can already get.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who face discrimination on the job because of race, sex, religion, national origin, disability, or age. Those who prove serious harm — lasting emotional distress, ruined careers — would no longer be limited to a fixed ceiling on compensation, and victims of age discrimination would gain remedies they have never had. The bill would also guarantee a jury trial in these cases, letting workers put their claim before a jury rather than a judge.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the tiered caps on compensatory and punitive damages in employment discrimination cases — currently $50,000 to $300,000 depending on employer size — so awards would reflect the actual harm a worker suffered rather than a statutory ceiling.

Makes victims of age discrimination eligible for the full range of legal and equitable relief available under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, which includes compensatory and punitive damages they currently cannot recover under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act.
Guarantees any party in a case under 42 U.S.C. 1981a may demand a jury trial, so workers are not forced to have their discrimination claim decided by a judge alone.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would face uncapped liability in discrimination suits — the largest exposure falling on big companies currently capped at $300,000 — plus higher litigation and settlement costs as cases become riskier to defend. Those costs could pass through to small businesses as well, since the caps that protected even the smallest employers would also disappear.

drawbacks.text: Uncapped compensatory and punitive damages would raise the cost and risk of defending any employment discrimination claim, a cost that lands heaviest on small businesses and can be passed on in wages or prices; the existing caps were enacted in the 1991 Civil Rights Act precisely to keep awards predictable.

A guaranteed jury trial in every case where one is demanded can make outcomes less predictable and lengthen litigation, since juries may award larger amounts than judges in emotionally charged discrimination cases.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers who endure serious on-the-job discrimination, the gain is real: the current $300,000 cap can undervalue a destroyed career or years of emotional harm, and age discrimination victims today cannot recover these damages at all. The cost is borne by employers, including small ones, in higher and less predictable legal exposure — an honest trade-off, but one weighted toward the workers the bill was written for.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees on the day it was introduced, and neither one ever held a hearing or sent it to the floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Suzanne Bonamici introduced the Equal Remedies Act of 2024 on May 8, 2024, joined by Representative Bobby Scott of Virginia.
Eleven additional Democratic representatives cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

The bill was referred the same day to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and the House Judiciary Committee, and the record shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers are better off because the bill died: their liability in discrimination lawsuits remains capped at $50,000–$300,000, and age discrimination plaintiffs still cannot recover compensatory or punitive damages. Workers who hoped for stronger remedies gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who kept damage caps in place

industries.industry: U.S. employers (all sizes, especially large companies)
industries.note: The bill would have removed the $50,000–$300,000 caps on compensatory and punitive damages in discrimination cases and extended uncapped-style remedies to age discrimination claims, exposing employers to larger verdicts and settlements. The industry's interest in keeping the caps runs against workers seeking full compensation for proven harm.

industries.industry: Management-side employment law and litigation costs
industries.note: Higher and less predictable damages would increase demand for defense counsel and drive up the cost of resolving discrimination claims for both sides. Employers' legal spending in this bill's world works to limit worker recoveries.
